label: GPT-6 Luna
output:
**Dear Jonno: the coolroom died on Cup Day**

Mate,

You keep asking what happened with the coolroom on Cup Day, so here it is in one convenient blog post instead of me trying to explain it between services and forgetting half the story.

First, a quick update from London: you’ve gone soft. I know you think you’d have been calm and useful in a crisis, but I reckon you’d have taken one look at the thermometer and started drafting a strongly worded message to the council. You would’ve lost your mind. Anyway, let me tell you how it went.

The compressor packed it in overnight between Monday and Tuesday. At 6.40 on Cup Day morning, we opened the coolroom and found the thermometer sitting at 11 degrees. Not “a bit warm in there.” Eleven. The sort of temperature where the fridge is less a fridge and more a large cupboard with ambitions.

And naturally, it was Cup Day. We had 140 covers booked for lunch, all on a three-course set menu. Nothing says “relaxed public holiday service” like discovering at sparrow’s fart that your main cold-storage situation has become a science experiment.

Raff was away, so I was running the show. The head chef being absent is usually fine. The head chef being absent on the morning the coolroom dies is when you start to understand why people believe in curses.

The first job was getting everything out of there and finding it somewhere else to live. We shifted stock into the two undercounters, the bar fridge, and half of Marta’s walk-in next door. Marta did us a massive favour, obviously, though she’s now collecting repayment in croissant credit. I owe her about three weeks of staff meal, so if she ever reads this: yes, I know. I’m not avoiding you. I’m just waiting for the croissants to stop compounding interest.

We lost about $1,800 in stock, mostly dairy and duck legs. A painful amount of money to watch go in the bin, but also a fairly good argument for not trusting a compressor to make it through a long weekend. The fridge guy, Wally from Coldline, couldn’t get to us until Wednesday, and the part had to come up from Sydney. So there we were: one dead coolroom, a packed lunch service, and a repair timeline that sounded like it had been organised by a carrier pigeon.

Then came the beef shin. Benny and I had to get 30 kilos of it down the laneway on a milk-crate trolley, in the rain. This is the sort of thing that sounds funny when you tell it later and feels less funny when you’re pushing a load of meat through a wet laneway on a trolley with one wheel that’s already making a noise.

Then the wheel fell off.

Not wobbled. Not got a bit loose. Fell off. There we were with 30 kilos of beef shin, rain coming down, and a trolley that had made a sudden and very clear decision to retire. I feel like this is the bit where you’d have asked whether we’d considered ordering an Uber XL.

Kev, meanwhile, was doing what Kev does best: getting on with it. He filled the old esky with ice from the servo. Fourteen bags of ice. The servo guy asked if we were having a party, which was a fair question, given the amount of ice and the general air of panic. I’m sure he thought we were either throwing the world’s saddest Cup Day barbecue or trying to preserve a body.

By the time lunch kicked off, everything that could be moved had been moved, everyone had a job, and the whole kitchen was running on bar fridges and spite. Phil popped in at some point and said, “Just make it work, mate.”

Thanks, Phil. Really useful. I’ll put it on the whiteboard next to “cook the food” and “don’t let the building fall down.”

At 12.15, we had to 86 the panna cotta. So dessert became “affogato with whatever.” Not exactly how we’d drawn it up, but people loved it more. Apparently, the secret to a popular dessert is to have a fridge die and then improvise under pressure. Maybe we should do that every week. (We won’t.)

A woman on table nine asked if the beef was “free range from the laneway” because she’d seen us hauling it past the window. I wanted to tell her it had a lovely life, mostly spent on a milk crate, but I think we just smiled and kept service moving.

And this, somehow, is the bit I’m proud of: everyone was locked in. Nobody melted down. We got through the 140 covers, the food went out, and the whole thing ended up being the best service we did all year. Not because anything went to plan, obviously. Nothing went to plan. But everyone pitched in, sorted whatever was in front of them, and kept going.

That’s bistro kitchens, I reckon. A lot of shouting, a lot of shifting things from one dodgy fridge to another, and a surprising amount of spite.

The universe did add one final joke, though. My horse in the sweep was called **Ice Cold Lad**. It came second last. After everything, I could’ve done with a winner. Instead, I got a horse whose name sounded like a promise and whose performance was more of a warning.

So that’s the story: a dead coolroom, 11 degrees, 140 lunches, 14 bags of servo ice, a one-wheeled trolley, an emergency dessert, and you safely on the other side of the world where nobody expects you to carry beef through a laneway in the rain.

Stay soft, London. We’ll keep the bar fridges warm for you.

Come home, ya flog.
